short: Vesuvius buried Pompeii, Herculaneum and Stabiae under ash and pyroclastic flows in a single eruption.
full:
Mount Vesuvius erupted with little warning, burying Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae and Oplontis under metres of ash, pumice and pyroclastic surges. Pliny the Younger, watching from Misenum, described a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine rising above the mountain before ash blotted out the sun; his uncle Pliny the Elder died attempting a rescue by sea. For centuries the eruption was dated to 24 August on the authority of Pliny's letters, but a charcoal graffito found in Pompeii referring to a date in mid-October, together with autumn produce found in the ruins, has led much recent scholarship toward a date in October instead.

Thousands died, entombed by ash that preserved buildings, wall paintings and the casts of victims' bodies with unusual fidelity. The buried towns were never resettled and were largely forgotten until excavations began in the eighteenth century, giving later archaeology an unmatched view of everyday life under the early Empire.
